name: recording-fake
intent: Give the system under test a collaborator that is both a working in-memory implementation and a journal of the operations it received, so a test can exercise real multi-step behaviour and then assert on the recorded interaction trace instead of on the double's return values.
problem: The behaviour under test is which operations the system under test performs on a collaborator - commands sent, records written, notifications dispatched, audit entries appended - and not the value it gets back or the state it leaves behind. A stub or mock records the calls but does not behave, so a multi-step flow (write then read, apply then compensate) cannot run against it; a plain fake behaves but records nothing, so the interaction the test cares about stays invisible. The recurring decision is how to keep working behaviour and observation in the same double without scripting an expectation list per test.
context: Unit and component tests around a system under test whose collaboration protocol is stateful and partly the specification, where the collaborator is substitutable (dependency injection, factory, registry or lookup) and the operations it receives have domain meaning worth asserting (deposits, commands, published events, audit entries). Typical in interaction-aware TDD of domain services and gateways, when a strict mock's expectations would be too rigid and a pure spy's recording without behaviour would not let the scenario run.
benefits: Behaviour and evidence in one double: the same object runs the sequence as a real (in-memory) collaborator and holds the journal that proves what the sequence was, so one test can assert both the resulting state and the interaction that produced it.

Assertions land on domain operations rather than raw call counts: a journal of typed entries (deposited, refunded, dispatched) reads like the requirement and survives signature-level refactoring better than argument matchers.

The recorded trace is deterministic and independent of a mocking framework: failures print the actual sequence, and the test can filter it by operation or compare it exactly where order is part of the contract.
One double serves many tests - the fake grows with the collaborator interface while the journal serves every interaction assertion - instead of a purpose-built expectation script per test.

State-based and interaction-based assertions cross-check each other in the same test, which exposes compensation and rollback bugs (a save followed by a delete, a publish that should not have happened) that either view alone would miss.
Works where no mocking framework is available or wanted (embedded C, plain Ruby, hand-rolled test rigs) and keeps the suite from depending on one library's verification DSL.
The journal doubles as a diagnostic artifact: when a test fails, the recorded operations usually explain the failure faster than a diff of expected versus actual calls.
tradeoffs: The double is a second implementation of the contract: building and maintaining both halves (behaviour and journal) costs more than a stub, and the fake's semantics can drift from the real collaborator, letting the suite stay green while production breaks.

Recording invites over-specification: asserting the whole journal, including incidental operations and their order, couples tests to the system under test's current algorithm, so refactorings fail even though the collaborator contract did not change (the Overspecified Software family of test smells).

Granularity is a real design decision: raw method calls are verbose and brittle, domain operations are stable but need mapping, and the wrong choice either hides the interaction that matters or bakes today's call pattern into the test.

The journal has a cost of its own: every operation allocates and is retained until the test ends, concurrent calls from the system under test race unless the journal is synchronized, and a double reused across tests leaks recorded history unless it is re-created or cleared.

Negative and cardinality constraints are weaker than with a mock: never called, exactly once and no unexpected call must be asserted by hand over the journal, and forgetting to assert them leaves the guarantee unproven while the test still passes.

A permissive fake can pass for the wrong reason: if it ignores uniqueness, validation or error paths the real collaborator enforces, the system under test's illegal sequence is accepted and the journal assertion is satisfied anyway.
The double never fails a test by itself - unlike a mock's verification, a journal that nobody reads is dead weight, and the assertion logic (and its maintenance) lives in the test code.

participants.responsibility: Test-only implementation of the collaborator's interface that really works (in-memory store, no I/O) and appends one typed journal entry per operation it receives.
Ordered, domain-level record of the operations received (operation kind plus arguments or resulting effect) kept inside the double; the artifact the test asserts against.

Test-facing methods or properties that expose the journal (all entries, entries filtered by operation, snapshots for order comparison); deliberately separate from the interface the system under test calls.
The production code under test, which calls the double through the collaborator interface and is unaware that its operations are being recorded.
The seam through which the double is installed (constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, test-specific subclass), matching how the system under test resolves its collaborators.
The production implementation whose semantics the fake approximates; kept in the suite by a contract or behaviour test so drift between fake and reality is detected.

Arranges the fake, exercises the system under test once, then asserts selectively over the journal and (optionally) over the resulting state; owns all assertion logic and resets the double between tests.

use_cases: An in-memory repository fake that journals save and delete operations, so a unit-of-work test can assert that exactly one aggregate was saved and then published while later reads still see the earlier writes.
A command driver fake for a device or external protocol that records open, write, flush and close in order, letting tests assert the wire-level sequence without hardware or a simulator.
A notification gateway fake that applies deduplication rules and journals each message, so the test asserts one notification per recipient while the actual policy code runs.
An audit sink fake in a security-sensitive service that stores entries for later reads and records every append, proving that each privileged operation produced an audit entry with the right actor.
A domain event publisher fake that journals published events in order and delivers them to in-memory subscribers, so tests assert the emitted event stream as well as the state change.
A cache-aside fake that records hits, misses and key accesses while actually caching, proving the read-through and write-through access pattern rather than only the final cached value.
A ledger or payment fake that journals deposits, withdrawals and reversals, so compensation logic is asserted as an interaction sequence (charge then refund) instead of as a final balance.

Rails Active Job's test adapter, which queues and records enqueued and performed jobs while tests can execute them, so an orchestration test can assert the job interaction trace without a production queue.

Django's locmem email backend, which accepts messages and stores them in django.core.mail.outbox, so application code exercises the sending path while tests inspect the recorded messages without external delivery.

An ASP.NET Core TestServer/WebApplicationFactory host, which runs the real request pipeline in memory and exposes an HttpClient, so integration tests can exercise behavior and inspect HTTP interactions without a network listener.
avoid_when: Only canned answers are needed and the interaction is not asserted: a stub (or a hard-coded test double such as a lambda or anonymous implementation) is simpler and cheaper.

The expected interaction is the specification and strictness matters (never called, exactly once, no unexpected call): a mock verifies that declaratively in the framework, and rebuilding those checks over a journal repeats work the library already did.
The double only needs to behave and the assertions are about resulting state: a plain fake without a journal, or a ready-made in-memory subsystem, is enough.
A single collaborator call is observed in one test: a framework spy or a captured callback is far less machinery than a journaling fake.

The real collaborator's semantics are the thing under test (query language, transactions, wire format): use a production-grade in-memory substitute plus contract or integration tests, not a hand-rolled recording fake.
The journal would be read by production code or the double shipped outside tests: an audit log in production is a domain feature with its own design, not a test double.
The test would compare the complete transcript of every call: assert selectively instead, or the double is doing the test's job and the suite becomes refactoring-hostile.
anti_patterns: A journal that is recorded but never asserted: the interaction evidence exists and the test still proves nothing about it.

Whole-transcript assertions that compare every recorded entry including incidental calls and exact order, pinning the system under test's current algorithm and breaking on behaviour-preserving refactorings.
Logging raw method calls or call counts instead of domain operations, so the journal mirrors the implementation's structure and ages with it.
Rebuilding a mocking framework inside the fake - expectation scripts, cardinality checks, a verification DSL - instead of using a mock library when strict verification is what the test needs.
A static, module-level or fixture-shared recording fake whose store and journal leak between tests, turning unrelated tests into order-dependent failures.
Recording interactions in the production collaborator (or in production code paths) to make tests observable, instead of keeping the journal in a test-only double.
Silent no-op methods for the operations the fake does not implement, so sequences succeed against a fake that no real collaborator would accept.
Unbounded journal growth in long or high-volume tests, occasionally burying the interesting operations and always costing memory.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the system under test depends on the collaborator's abstraction, which is what allows a recording double to be substituted at all.
Single responsibility: working behaviour, recording and retrieval are distinct responsibilities - the fake implements the collaborator's contract, the journal records, the accessors expose.
Interface segregation: the retrieval interface the test uses is separate from the collaborator interface the system under test sees, so recording facilities never leak into production code.
Separation of concerns: assertion logic stays in the test; the double only behaves and observes.
Don't repeat yourself: one recording fake shared across tests replaces a purpose-built expectation script per scenario.

Liskov substitutability as fidelity: the fake must honour the same observable contract as the real collaborator - state transitions, error semantics, ordering constraints - or assertions over its behaviour are meaningless.
You aren't gonna need it / KISS: journal only the operations the tests assert on, at the granularity that reads like the requirement.
best_practices: Record typed, domain-level operations (values or records), not raw call tuples or strings; the journal is an assertion surface and should read like the requirement.
Expose the journal through a test-only accessor interface, never through the collaborator interface the system under test consumes.
Re-create the fake per test or clear both store and journal explicitly; never keep mutable double state in static fields, globals or shared fixtures.
Validate the fake against the real collaborator with a shared contract or behaviour test (a verified fake), so behaviour drift fails loudly.
Assert selectively: filter the journal by operation and compare order only where order is part of the collaborator's contract.
Fail loudly on operations the fake does not implement (throw or panic) instead of silently succeeding, so the fake cannot certify sequences the real collaborator rejects.
Hand out defensive copies or immutable snapshots of the journal, and synchronize it when the system under test may call concurrently.
Leave strict cardinality and negative expectations (never called, exactly once) to a mock framework when they are the point, instead of rebuilding them over the journal.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Test Double Patterns: Fake Object (a much lighter-weight implementation, p. 551) and Test Spy (use a double to capture the indirect output calls made by the system under test for later verification); a recording fake is the composition of the two.
